desc:
A website logs how many people visited it on each of n days: visitors[i] is the count for day i. A day is record-breaking when both conditions hold:

  • its count is strictly larger than the count of every earlier day (day 0 has no earlier days, so this part is true for it), and
  • it is the last day, or its count is strictly larger than the count of the next day.

Return the number of record-breaking days.

Example: visitors = [1, 2, 0, 7, 2, 0, 2, 2] returns 2. Day 1 (count 2) beats day 0 and day 2; day 3 (count 7) beats everything before and after. Day 0 does not beat day 1, and the 2s later are not above the record 7.
hints: Checking each day against all earlier days works in O(n<sup>2</sup>). What single number summarises 'all earlier days'?
Keep the maximum count of the days before the current one. A day beats all earlier days exactly when it is above that maximum.
While scanning, compare visitors[i] with the running maximum and also with visitors[i + 1] (when it exists). Update the running maximum after the check.
editorial: Beating every earlier day is the same as beating the largest earlier day, so carry a running maximum best (initially below any valid count, for example -1). On day i, the day is a record if visitors[i] > best and (i is last or visitors[i] > visitors[i + 1]). After the test, set best = max(best, visitors[i]).

Strictness matters. Two days with the same count do not break each other's record, so a plateau such as [5, 5, 5] has zero record days. Because the running maximum only grows, a record day is also always a new running maximum, which is why the sequence of records is increasing.
One pass, O(n) time and O(1) space.
